client: I've been really struggling since my grandma passed away last month. At work, I'll just zone out staring at my computer and then realize I haven't gotten anything done for like an hour. The sadness comes in waves and it's hard to predict when it'll hit me.
therapist: I'm so sorry for your loss - it sounds like you're going through a really difficult time of grief, and those waves of sadness and difficulty concentrating are completely normal parts of the process. What thoughts tend to come up for you during those moments when you find yourself zoning out?

client: I keep thinking about all the things I should have said to her before she passed. Like there were so many conversations we never got to have. And then I feel guilty when I remember times I was too busy with work to visit her. It just plays on loop in my head.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of "what ifs" and regrets, which can feel so heavy when we're grieving. Let's explore those thoughts - when you think about being too busy with work, what evidence do you have that shows you still cared deeply for your grandma and made efforts to be there for her?

client: I did visit her every Sunday for brunch when I could...and I always called her on Wednesdays. But I guess I'm focusing on the times I canceled plans because of work deadlines. It's like those few times outweigh all the good ones in my mind right now.
therapist: I notice how your mind is magnifying those few canceled visits while minimizing all the consistent love and care you showed her week after week. That's a very common pattern when we're grieving - our brains tend to focus on what feels unfinished. What would you say to a friend who was being this hard on themselves about showing up for someone they loved?

client: I'd probably tell them they did the best they could and that their loved one knew they cared. But when I try to say that to myself, it feels different - like I should have done more somehow. It's hard to let go of that guilt even though logically I know I showed up for her in lots of ways.
therapist: It's interesting how we can offer compassion to others so easily, yet struggle to extend that same kindness to ourselves. That disconnect between what we know logically and what we feel emotionally is so human, especially in grief. What might it feel like to try writing a letter to yourself from your grandma's perspective, imagining what she might say about those times you showed up for her?

client: The idea of writing a letter from her perspective makes me feel both hopeful and nervous. I worry that I won't be able to imagine her words accurately, and that I'll just end up feeling more guilty if I can't get it "right." At the same time, part of me wonders if it might help me focus on the positive memories instead of just the regrets.
therapist: It makes complete sense that this exercise brings up both hope and nervousness - grief work often holds that mix of emotions. What if we took the pressure off getting it "right," and instead approached this as an experiment where the goal is simply to notice what comes up, without judgment?

client: Taking the pressure off feels a little easier to consider. I guess I'm still worried that even if I try this, I might end up focusing on the negative memories instead of the positive ones. It's like my mind automatically goes to what I did wrong rather than what I did right, even if I try to steer it differently.
therapist: That automatic pull toward negative memories is exactly what we're trying to gently understand and shift - not by forcing positivity, but by creating space for all your memories to coexist. Could we try starting with just one small positive memory of your time together, and see what that brings up for you?

client: I remember how she used to make my favorite cookies whenever I visited, even when I got older. That makes me smile, but then I feel guilty because I didn't tell her enough how much I appreciated those little things. It's like even the happy memories bring up regrets now.
therapist: It's beautiful that you're holding onto those warm memories of her care for you, and I hear how the regret sneaks in even there. This mix of joy and pain is so common - the love and the loss existing together. What do you think your grandma would say about you remembering these small, loving gestures now?

client: She'd probably say she knew I appreciated her without me having to say it all the time...she was always pretty intuitive like that. But part of me still feels like I should have expressed it more. It's confusing because logically I know she felt loved, but emotionally I still feel like I failed her in some way.
therapist: That tension between what you know intellectually and what you feel emotionally is where so much of grief resides. It sounds like you're beginning to recognize your grandma's perspective - that love often doesn't need constant verbal confirmation to be deeply felt. What might it feel like to sit with both truths: that you showed love in your own ways, while also making space for that very human wish to have done more?

client: That actually makes me tear up a little - the idea that both things can be true at once. It feels like I'm either a good granddaughter or a terrible one in my mind, with no in-between. Maybe allowing both truths would take some of the sharp edges off this grief, but it's scary to let go of the self-blame because that's felt like honoring her somehow.
therapist: It's so meaningful that you can recognize how the self-blame has felt like a way to honor her - we often hold onto guilt as a misplaced form of loyalty to those we've lost. What if honoring her could also look like embracing the full truth of your relationship, with all its beautiful imperfections?

client: That idea makes me feel both relieved and uncomfortable at the same time. Part of me wants to hold onto the guilt because it feels like the only way to keep her memory alive, but another part knows she wouldn't want me to punish myself like this. It's just hard to imagine grieving without the self-blame - that feels foreign and almost disrespectful somehow.
therapist: That's such an honest and insightful recognition - how the guilt has become intertwined with keeping her memory alive. It might help to remember that love and grief don't require punishment to be valid; your relationship was real regardless of whether you carry this pain. What small step could you take this week to honor her memory in a way that feels more aligned with the love you shared?
